title: Treasury yields steady after inflation warning from New York Fed's Williams, investors await 5-year auction
html:
U.S. Treasury yields inched lower on Tuesday as investors took stock of a speech by John Williams of the New York Fed and looked ahead to a 5-year bond auction due later in the session.

The 10-year Treasury yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, student loans and credit card debt — was down 1 basis point at 4.908%.

The 2-year Treasury note yield, the most sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was steady at 4.660%. The 30-year Treasury yield — which often reacts the most to geopolitical developments — was down 1 basis point at 5.285%

One basis point equals 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.

Monetary policy will need to adjust to "get inflation back to our 2% goal in a timely manner and on a sustained basis," Williams, president and chief executive of the New York Fed, said on Monday.

"There is still work to do to get that done," Williams added in comments at the University of Mount Saint Vincent in New York.

He said the latest economic data shows "the economy has remained strong and that inflation has continued to run too high."

William's comments come ahead of the December FOMC meeting on 8-9 December. Investors are now pricing in a 100% chance of another interest rate hike, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool, with a 25 basis point increase expected.

Later on Tuesday, investors will be watching a $70 billion 5-year Treasury auction as the latest supply test, as well as the consumer confidence print for November. The October reading of the personal consumption expenditures price index, which measures underlying inflation, is due Wednesday. A rise of 0.3% is expected, according to economists polled by Dow Jones.

Revised GDP data, also due on Wednesday, is expected to confirm that the U.S. economy expanded by 3.4% in the third quarter, according to Trading Economics forecasts. This compares to 2.2% growth in the second quarter.
summary: U.S. Treasury yields were broadly flat on Tuesday as investors took stock of a speech by John Williams of the New York Fed.
